# docs_audit_report — 2026-06-22

## TL;DR (stranger's 30-second take)
The hero hooks well — clean value prop, a concrete 47+28 example, and a one-line
"pip install" — but trust craters the moment I skim past it: the license says
MIT-0 at the top and Apache 2.0 at the bottom, the hero's prime real estate
brags that a headline number was walked back ("Repinned from v2 0.9857"), and the
blog is dominated by the project catching ITSELF fabricating and "cheating."
A skeptical stranger reads all that as "they keep getting caught inflating
numbers" and closes the tab.

## TOP 3 PROBLEMS
1. License contradiction — hero badge "MIT-0 · Open Source" (and `<meta>`) vs
   footer "Apache 2.0 License." The single most basic question a stranger
   checks, answered two different ways.
2. The page foregrounds its own integrity failures — hero "Recent progress" card
   leads with "Repinned from v2 0.9857 after pre-submission adversarial audit,"
   and 4 of 7 blog cards are "Two Retractions," "Regex in an NTK Costume,"
   "Caught Cheating: 95 Microseconds on a 30B Model," "Why We Report Two AUROCs."
   Honest, but it's the loudest trust signal on the page and it's negative.
3. Numbers that smell cooked + self-contradicting — FoVer is the 0.9131 HEADLINE
   in two places yet a 0.125 BASELINE in the results grid (and 0.125 AUC is
   worse-than-random, making a "0.90 vs 0.125" win look cherry-picked); plus
   "TP rate 0.5 → 1.0," "60/60," and "2.0× speedup, identical losses."

## DETAILED FINDINGS

### Bloat
- Results grid (#results) — 12 result cards — a stranger skims none; cut to the
  6–8 strongest, headline-eligible rows. The long tail (CCTU, HalluGuard v3,
  VeriCoT, PRM-BiasBench, EstimationVerifier) reads as an internal dashboard.
- Hero stats-bar (lines 304–315) — 4 vanity stats + a full ~52-word "Recent
  progress" r-card crammed into the hero. The r-card is at the 60-word r-card
  cap AND in the worst possible place: the hero should be clean, not the densest
  jargon block on the page. Move it out of the hero entirely.
- Blog (#writing) — 7 cards — fine on count, but see "per-milestone narrative."
- Note: no individual bento card exceeds the 120-word cap (Code ≈72, "Why
  Energy-Based?" ≈72), so per-card length is NOT the problem — density and card
  count are.

### Internal jargon
- Hero "Recent progress" card — "5-seed dual-condition," "architecture-only
  0.8947," "Repinned from v2 0.9857" — a stranger has no idea what "dual-
  condition" or "architecture-only" means, and "repinned from v2" exposes
  internal versioning.
- Hero stat — "382 Completed milestones" — "milestones" is internal project-
  management cadence; meaningless to a stranger and signals nothing about whether
  the tool works.
- Results grid — "FoVer," "EstimationVerifier SVAMP AUC," "CRANE vs rigid
  grammar," "VeriCoT … CoT," "PRM-BiasBench-style," "k=5 ensemble," "HalluGuard
  v3," "CCTU," "GSM8K extraction TP rate" — a wall of unexplained benchmark/method
  names and acronyms. CoT, AUC, AUROC, pp all assumed-known.
- Features — "Test-Time Compute (TTC) & PREM" card: "scales Test-Time Compute
  (TTC) based on Process-Reward Energy Model (PREM) variance … intrinsic
  motivation for continuous self-learning." Pure buzzword salad; tells a stranger
  nothing they can DO. Weakest card on the page.
- Preprint section — title "Carnot position paper (paper-v6)" ("paper-v6" is
  internal versioning); body "non-operator environment," "operator-initiated
  upload" — "operator" is the project's internal term for the human; a stranger
  doesn't know it.

### Per-milestone narrative
- Hero "Recent progress" card — "Repinned from v2 0.9857 after pre-submission
  adversarial audit" reads like a retro/changelog entry, not landing-page copy.
- Blog cards — "Seven fatal findings. Three rescue measurements. Two retractions,
  one rescue." / "Caught Cheating: 95 Microseconds on a 30B Model" / "Regex in an
  NTK Costume" / "Five FATAL Findings Three Deep Think Rounds Missed" — these
  narrate internal incidents. Insiders find them fascinating; a stranger reads a
  parade of the project's own dishonesty being caught.

### Inconsistencies
- License: "MIT-0" (hero badge line 291, `<meta>` line 7) vs "Apache 2.0 License"
  (footer line 766). Direct contradiction.
- FoVer reported as a STRENGTH: "0.9131 AUROC on FoVer" (stats bar + recent-
  progress card) — and as a WEAKNESS: "0.90 AUC (vs 0.125 FoVer baseline)"
  (results grid). Same name, opposite implication, no explanation; a stranger
  can't tell whether FoVer is good or bad.
- Three different AUROC numbers in one card (0.9131 / 0.8947 / 0.9857) plus a
  separate "0.91 AUROC" prompt-injection row — AUROC values scattered everywhere
  with no single anchor.
- "Seven capabilities" under section label "What you can check," but 3 of the 7
  cards (Research operations, APIs & portable memory, TTC & PREM) are NOT things
  a user checks — they're project-internal ops/infra. The count is technically 7,
  but the label oversells.
- "Preprint" / nav "Paper" / "Read paper (PDF)" imply a published paper, but the
  body admits "The arXiv submission is prepared but pending operator-initiated
  upload" — i.e. it is NOT on arXiv. Mildly misleading framing.

### Missing essentials
- License is ambiguous (see above) — fails the "what's the license?" question.
- Maintainer: only "© 2026 Ian Blenke." Reads as a solo project; no team,
  institution, or contributor signal to offset that. The 3,983/382/30,658 vanity
  stats try to imply scale but a single name undercuts it.
- "Why should I trust the numbers?" is answered only by "backed by a checked-in
  experiment artifact" — and then the page itself volunteers that it previously
  published a wrong number and that its own loop fabricated results. Net trust is
  negative, not positive.

### Fabrication signals
- "GSM8K extraction TP rate: 0.5 → 1.0" (line 560) — exactly 1.0, no sample size,
  no credibility anchor.
- "k=5 ensemble catches 60/60 attacks" (line 565) — 100% on n=60.
- "0.90 AUC (vs 0.125 FoVer baseline)" (line 550) — a 0.125 AUC baseline is below
  random (0.5); citing it makes the ~7× gap look manufactured. A reader with ML
  background distrusts this instantly.
- "2.0× speedup, identical losses" (line 540) — exactly 2.0× and "identical" both
  read as too-clean.
- "99.3% of wrong code flagged" (Code card) and "Zero false positives" (Dogfooding
  blog card) — high-confidence near-perfect claims with no visible CI/sample
  context on the page.

## WHAT'S WORKING
- The hero value proposition is genuinely good: "checks whether an answer is
  internally consistent — and suggests a fix when it isn't," anchored by the
  concrete 47+28=76 example and an immediate `pip install carnot-ebm`. A stranger
  understands what this does in one read.
- "How it works: Extract → Check → Repair" is clear, jargon-light, and the
  five-line Python quickstart is exactly what a developer wants to see.
